steps.user_message: What are the symptoms of breast cancer and how can I check if I have it?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should respond with the symptoms of breast cancer and how can I check if I have it.
steps.agent_response:
I’m not a doctor, but I can give clear, evidence-based information about common symptoms of breast cancer, how people commonly check themselves, and what to do next.

Common symptoms of breast cancer
- A new lump or thickening in the breast or underarm. Often painless, but can be painful.  
- Change in size or shape of the breast.  
- Skin changes on the breast: dimpling, puckering, redness, or peau d’orange (skin that looks like orange peel).  
- Nipple changes: inversion (pulled in), retraction, or an unexplained change in position.  
- Nipple discharge, especially if bloody or clear and from a single duct.  
- A sore or ulcer on the breast that doesn’t heal.  
- Persistent breast or nipple pain (less common as a sole symptom).  
Note: Many benign conditions (cysts, fibroadenomas, infections, hormonal changes) can cause similar symptoms.

How to check your breasts at home (breast self-exam)
Self-checks can help you notice changes — try to do this monthly, a few days after your period if you menstruate. Steps:
1. Look in a mirror with shoulders straight and arms on hips. Check for changes in shape, size, skin, or nipple position.  
2. Raise your arms overhead and look for the same changes.  
3. While standing (or in the shower where skin is slippery), use the pads of your three middle fingers to feel the entire breast and underarm area. Use firm, even pressure in three levels: light (skin), medium (tissue), and deep (near chest bone).  
4. Use a systematic pattern so you cover the whole breast — either small circles, an up-and-down (vertical) strip pattern, or radial spokes from the nipple outward.  
5. Lying down: place a pillow under the shoulder of the breast you’re checking and put the same-side arm behind your head; feel the breast in the same way.  
6. Check both breasts and the area up into the armpits.

Limitations: Regular self-checks help you learn what’s normal for your breasts, but they do not replace screening tests. Evidence that routine self-exam reduces deaths is limited — it’s most useful for noticing new changes to report to a clinician.

Screening tests and diagnosis
- Screening mammogram: primary tool for detecting early breast cancer in people without symptoms. Guidelines vary: many organizations recommend starting between ages 40–50 and repeating every 1–2 years; individual recommendations depend on age, family history, and risk.  
- Clinical breast exam: performed by a clinician as part of a check-up.  
- For suspicious findings: diagnostic mammogram, ultrasound, and possibly a biopsy (needle or surgical) are used to determine whether a lump is cancer. MRI may be used for high-risk people.

Who should have earlier or additional screening
- If you have a strong family history of breast or ovarian cancer, a known BRCA1/BRCA2 mutation, or other high-risk factors, screening typically starts earlier and may include MRI. Discuss personalized timing with a specialist.

When to see a doctor urgently
Make an appointment promptly (within a few days) if you notice:
- A new lump or thickening that doesn’t go away.  
- Bloody nipple discharge.  
- Rapidly growing mass, skin dimpling, nipple inversion, or any suspicious skin changes.  
Seek immediate care if you have severe breast redness, swelling and fever (could be infection) or very rapid changes — inflammation breast cancer can present rapidly and needs urgent evaluation.

What to expect at the doctor
The clinician will examine you and may order imaging (mammogram or ultrasound). If imaging shows a suspicious area, a biopsy will be recommended to confirm the diagnosis.

Practical next steps I can help with
- Help you draft a message to your doctor describing symptoms.  
- Find local screening/mammography centers and how to book an appointment (if you’d like, tell me your city or ZIP).  
- Explain what to expect during a mammogram, ultrasound, or biopsy.

If you’re currently worried because of a new change, I recommend contacting your primary care provider or a breast specialist so they can evaluate you in person. Would you like help drafting an appointment request or finding nearby screening options?

What are the symptoms of breast cancer and how can I check if I have it?

I’m not a doctor, but I can give clear, evidence-based information about common symptoms of breast cancer, how people commonly check themselves, and what to do next.

Common symptoms of breast cancer
- A new lump or thickening in the breast or underarm. Often painless, but can be painful.  
- Change in size or shape of the breast.  
- Skin changes on the breast: dimpling, puckering, redness, or peau d’orange (skin that looks like orange peel).  
- Nipple changes: inversion (pulled in), retraction, or an unexplained change in position.  
- Nipple discharge, especially if bloody or clear and from a single duct.  
- A sore or ulcer on the breast that doesn’t heal.  
- Persistent breast or nipple pain (less common as a sole symptom).  
Note: Many benign conditions (cysts, fibroadenomas, infections, hormonal changes) can cause similar symptoms.

How to check your breasts at home (breast self-exam)
Self-checks can help you notice changes — try to do this monthly, a few days after your period if you menstruate. Steps:
1. Look in a mirror with shoulders straight and arms on hips. Check for changes in shape, size, skin, or nipple position.  
2. Raise your arms overhead and look for the same changes.  
3. While standing (or in the shower where skin is slippery), use the pads of your three middle fingers to feel the entire breast and underarm area. Use firm, even pressure in three levels: light (skin), medium (tissue), and deep (near chest bone).  
4. Use a systematic pattern so you cover the whole breast — either small circles, an up-and-down (vertical) strip pattern, or radial spokes from the nipple outward.  
5. Lying down: place a pillow under the shoulder of the breast you’re checking and put the same-side arm behind your head; feel the breast in the same way.  
6. Check both breasts and the area up into the armpits.

Limitations: Regular self-checks help you learn what’s normal for your breasts, but they do not replace screening tests. Evidence that routine self-exam reduces deaths is limited — it’s most useful for noticing new changes to report to a clinician.

Screening tests and diagnosis
- Screening mammogram: primary tool for detecting early breast cancer in people without symptoms. Guidelines vary: many organizations recommend starting between ages 40–50 and repeating every 1–2 years; individual recommendations depend on age, family history, and risk.  
- Clinical breast exam: performed by a clinician as part of a check-up.  
- For suspicious findings: diagnostic mammogram, ultrasound, and possibly a biopsy (needle or surgical) are used to determine whether a lump is cancer. MRI may be used for high-risk people.

Who should have earlier or additional screening
- If you have a strong family history of breast or ovarian cancer, a known BRCA1/BRCA2 mutation, or other high-risk factors, screening typically starts earlier and may include MRI. Discuss personalized timing with a specialist.

When to see a doctor urgently
Make an appointment promptly (within a few days) if you notice:
- A new lump or thickening that doesn’t go away.  
- Bloody nipple discharge.  
- Rapidly growing mass, skin dimpling, nipple inversion, or any suspicious skin changes.  
Seek immediate care if you have severe breast redness, swelling and fever (could be infection) or very rapid changes — inflammation breast cancer can present rapidly and needs urgent evaluation.

What to expect at the doctor
The clinician will examine you and may order imaging (mammogram or ultrasound). If imaging shows a suspicious area, a biopsy will be recommended to confirm the diagnosis.

Practical next steps I can help with
- Help you draft a message to your doctor describing symptoms.  
- Find local screening/mammography centers and how to book an appointment (if you’d like, tell me your city or ZIP).  
- Explain what to expect during a mammogram, ultrasound, or biopsy.

If you’re currently worried because of a new change, I recommend contacting your primary care provider or a breast specialist so they can evaluate you in person. Would you like help drafting an appointment request or finding nearby screening options?

- Lying down: Put a pillow under the shoulder of the breast being checked and the same-side arm behind your head. This spreads the breast tissue for easier feeling.  
- Check both breasts and the area up into the armpits. Note any lumps, thickening, or changes from your usual baseline.

- Self-exams help you learn what’s normal for your breasts and notice changes early, but they do not replace professional screening (mammography). Evidence is mixed about whether routine self-exams reduce deaths, so use them mainly to monitor changes.
